faq.a: Early antibiotics reduce mortality; cultures rarely change initial choice in typical settings.
faq.q: Why give amoxicillin before waiting for cultures?

faq.a: Yes, malaria can present with fever and respiratory symptoms, but lack of focal lung findings and normal chest X‑ray help differentiate.
faq.q: Can malaria cause a similar fever‑cough picture?

faq.a: In clear clinical pneumonia with limited resources, treat empirically; X‑ray is reserved for atypical presentation or treatment failure.
faq.q: When is a chest X‑ray not needed?

exam: A 45‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with fever, cough, and SpO2 88% — what immediate steps and why? — Give oxygen, start empiric ampicillin‑clavulanate, assess severity with CURB‑65, arrange admission.

You have a patient with tachypnea, dullness to percussion at the right base, but no X‑ray — how do you confirm consolidation? — Perform bedside lung ultrasound (if available) or rely on clinical signs; treat as pneumonia.
Why is monotherapy with azithromycin discouraged in East African settings? — High macrolide resistance among S. pneumoniae; it may lead to treatment failure.
A child with sickle cell disease develops fever and cough; what extra considerations? — Higher risk of pneumococcal infection, consider broader coverage and ensure vaccination status.
How does CURB‑65 guide admission decisions in low‑resource hospitals? — Score ≥2 indicates need for inpatient care; it uses readily available data.
What complication should you monitor for after 48 h of therapy? — Development of empyema or lung abscess; look for persistent fever, pleural effusion, or worsening infiltrates.
If a patient cannot tolerate oral meds, what IV option is appropriate and why? — IV ampicillin‑clavulanate provides similar coverage without risking oral absorption issues.
Explain why a normal white cell count does not rule out bacterial pneumonia in a malnourished patient — Malnutrition blunts inflammatory response; rely on clinical picture and other investigations.
ai.title: Bacterial Pneumonia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Acute infection of the lung parenchyma caused by bacteria, common in low‑resource settings. Diagnosis relies on clinical syndrome plus limited investigations; early antibiotics and supportive care are lifesaving.

b: Rapid onset fever, chills, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain
Tachypnea, hypoxia, crackles on auscultation
May present with confusion in the elderly or children
sections.p: Bacterial pneumonia is an acute infection of the alveoli and interstitium, leading to consolidation, impaired gas exchange and systemic inflammation. In East Africa, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus and Gram‑negative bacilli dominate, especially in patients with HIV, malnutrition or recent malaria.

b: S. pneumoniae: most common, sensitive to penicillin unless resistant
H. influenzae: often beta‑lactamase producing, requires ampicillin‑clavulanate
Staphylococcus aureus: post‑influenza, may cause empyema
sections.p: Typical bacteria are encapsulated Gram‑positive diplococci (S. pneumoniae) or non‑encapsulated Gram‑negative rods (H. influenzae). Virulence factors include capsule (evasion of phagocytosis), pneumolysin (lung injury) and beta‑lactamase (antibiotic resistance).

b: Crowded living conditions and poor ventilation increase risk
HIV and malnutrition reduce mucosal immunity
sections.p: Bacteria spread by respiratory droplets; colonisation of the nasopharynx precedes aspiration into the lower airway, especially during viral upper‑respiratory infection or impaired cough reflex.

b: Mild: fever, cough, localized crackles, normal oxygen saturation
Moderate: tachypnea >30/min, SpO2 90‑94%, chest X‑ray consolidation
Severe: respiratory rate >30/min, SpO2 <90%, hypotension, altered mental status
sections.p: Clinical syndrome ranges from mild, outpatient‑treated disease to severe, life‑threatening pneumonia with sepsis and respiratory failure.
Combine bedside assessment with the few investigations usually available in low‑resource hospitals.

t.b: Confirms consolidation; helps differentiate from TB or pulmonary oedema
Answers if hypoxia is present; SpO2 <90% indicates need for supplemental O2
Leukocytosis with neutrophilia supports bacterial cause; may be normal in HIV

t.a: Sputum Gram stain / culture (if lab exists)
t.b: Identifies organism and resistance; if unavailable, treat empirically
Detects underlying immunosuppression that alters pathogen spectrum

b: First‑line: amoxicillin (covers S. pneumoniae) or ampicillin‑clavulanate (covers H. influenzae)
If severe or risk of MRSA: add cloxacillin or consider vancomycin where available
Avoid macrolides as monotherapy in areas with high resistance
Supportive: oxygen to keep SpO2 ≥ 94%, IV fluids for sepsis, analgesia
If no X‑ray, treat based on clinical criteria (cough, fever, tachypnea, crackles)
Vaccination (pneumococcal, Hib) for prevention
sections.p: Start empiric antibiotics within one hour of recognition, then adjust when microbiology results return. Provide supportive care and monitor for complications.

b: Use CURB‑65 (Confusion, Urea, Respiratory rate, Blood pressure, age ≥65) to decide admission; score ≥2 → admit
In HIV, consider atypical organisms (Pneumocystis, TB) if no response to antibiotics
Empyema suspicion: persistent fever, pleural effusion on X‑ray → thoracentesis
sections.p: Key points examiners love: pattern recognition, severity scoring, rational antibiotic choice, and recognising red‑flags.

whenToSeekHelp: Systolic BP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 mmHg
